cards.title: EV charging hub
cards.prompt: Design the classes for an electric vehicle charging hub. It has bays with chargers of different speeds, drivers can reserve a bay or walk in, and there's an idle fee if a car stays plugged in after charging ends.
brief_lines: Bays with chargers of different speeds
facts_if_asked: Three charger speeds: standard, fast and ultra.
A reservation holds a bay for fifteen minutes past its start time, then expires.
The idle fee starts five minutes after charging completes, charged per minute.
Price per kilowatt hour depends on charger speed.
One hub, one process; ignore networking and payments processing.
follow_ups: What states does a charging session go through?
Two drivers try to take the last free bay at once. What happens?
cards.twist: The hub adds off peak pricing: cheaper rates between ten at night and six in the morning. What changes in your model?
hints: Talk me through what a driver does from arriving to leaving.
What are the main things that exist at the hub, and what does each one know?
What changes over the life of a single charge?
What if the session were its own class with states, and pricing lived behind its own interface?
strong_answer_covers: Hub, Bay, Charger with a speed type, Reservation, ChargingSession, Driver or Vehicle
PricingPolicy as an interface or strategy, chosen per charger speed
ChargingSession as a state machine: reserved, charging, complete, idle, closed
Fee calculation from energy used plus idle minutes, in one place
Bay allocation guarded for concurrent requests
Off peak extension as a new pricing policy without editing sessions

cards.title: Library holds
cards.prompt: Design the classes for a library system where members borrow books, place holds on titles that are out, and pay fines for late returns.
facts_if_asked: A title can have several physical copies.
Loans last three weeks.
When a copy is returned and someone holds the title, it's kept for that person for three days.
Fines are twenty five cents a day, capped at ten dollars per loan.
Members can have at most five loans and three holds.
follow_ups: What's the difference between a title and a copy in your model?
Where does the hold queue live?
Two members try to claim the last copy at the same moment. What happens?
cards.twist: The library adds e-books with a licence that allows only five loans at once. How does your model take it?
hints: Talk me through what happens when a member walks in to borrow a book.
When a book is out, what does the member actually wait for: that copy, or any copy?
Where would the line of waiting members be kept?
What if Title and Copy were separate classes and each Title had its own hold queue?
strong_answer_covers: Title versus Copy split
Member, Loan, Hold, HoldQueue per Title
FinePolicy in one place, with the cap
Return flow: copy goes to the next hold, with a pickup deadline
Claiming a copy is atomic or locked
E-books through a shared Lendable interface or licence policy, without special cases everywhere
Holds go on titles, not specific copies; fine logic lives in one place

cards.title: Trip expense splitter
cards.prompt: Design the classes for an app where friends on a trip log shared expenses, split them equally, by exact amounts or by percentage, and then see who owes whom with as few payments as possible.
brief_lines: Split equally, by exact amounts, or by percent
facts_if_asked: One currency per trip.
Amounts are in cents; splits must add up to the total.
Rounding leftovers go to the person who paid.
Expenses can be edited or deleted.
Groups of up to twenty people.
follow_ups: Where does the split rule live?
How do you handle a total that doesn't divide evenly?
How do you compute who owes whom?
What happens to balances when an expense is edited?
cards.twist: The app adds recurring expenses, like a shared rent payment every month. What changes?
hints: Talk me through what happens when someone logs a dinner bill.
What are the different ways to split, and what do they have in common?
What do you need to know at the end: every expense, or each person's net balance?
What if each split type were its own strategy, and a ledger kept net balances?
strong_answer_covers: Trip, Member, Expense, Split strategies for equal, exact and percent
Validation that splits add up, in cents
A stated rounding rule
Ledger of net balances updated per expense, recomputed on edit
Settlement by matching largest debtor with largest creditor
Recurring expenses as a schedule that creates expenses, not a new split type

cards.title: Coffee kiosk
cards.prompt: Design the classes for a self service coffee kiosk: customers order drinks from recipes, the kiosk tracks ingredients, handles items running out, and can be put into maintenance mode.
facts_if_asked: Recipes list ingredients with amounts, like eighteen grams of beans and two hundred millilitres of milk.
Customers can add extra shots or swap milk types.
Ingredients are reserved when an order is paid and used when the drink is made.
Staff get alerted when any ingredient drops below ten percent.
In maintenance mode, no new orders are accepted, but the drink in progress finishes.
follow_ups: What happens if an ingredient runs out between ordering and making?
Where do the kiosk's modes live?
How do staff get told about low stock?
How do customisations fit the recipe model?
cards.twist: The kiosk adds a seasonal drink that is only available in certain months. How do you add it?
hints: Talk me through a customer ordering a latte with oat milk.
What changes about the kiosk's behaviour between normal and maintenance mode?
When should ingredients be taken out of the inventory?
What if the inventory had reserve and commit steps, and the kiosk's mode were a state object?
strong_answer_covers: Recipe, Ingredient, Inventory, Order, Customisation
Inventory with reserve, commit and release
Kiosk modes as a state pattern: ready, making, maintenance, out of order
Low stock alerts through an observer or event
Customisations as recipe modifiers rather than new recipes
Seasonal drinks through an availability rule on the recipe
